title: The Doctrine of Sanctification: Westminster Confession Chapter 13, Paragraph 1
speaker: Mr. Alex Lyro

outline.title: Definition and Scope of Sanctification
subpoints: Sanctification is God's lifelong work of renewing the whole person into the image of Christ.
It is distinct from justification, which is a legal declaration of righteousness.
Sanctification is a transformation of character and conduct, not just standing.

outline.title: Who is Sanctified?
subpoints: Only those who are effectually called, regenerated, and justified.
Sanctification is not for everyone, but for those God has chosen and brought to life.
The distinction between justification and sanctification prevents legalism and antinomianism.

outline.title: The Foundation of Sanctification
subpoints: Rooted in the virtue of Christ's death and resurrection.
Powered by the Holy Spirit, not human willpower or discipline.
Believers are united to Christ in His death and resurrection, enabling newness of life.

outline.title: The Internal Work of the Holy Spirit
subpoints: God creates a new heart and new spirit in the believer.
This results in a genuine desire for God and holiness, distinct from previous spiritual death.
The ongoing conflict with sin indicates spiritual life, not death.

summary:
This lesson continues the study of the Order of Salvation by examining the doctrine of sanctification as presented in Chapter 13, Paragraph 1 of the Westminster Confession of Faith. The speaker defines sanctification as God's gracious, lifelong work of renewing the whole person into the image of Christ through union with Him and the power of the Holy Spirit. It is emphasized that sanctification is distinct from justification; while justification changes a believer's legal standing before God through imputed righteousness, sanctification transforms their character and conduct through the indwelling of the Holy Spirit.

The teaching clarifies that sanctification is reserved for those who have been effectually called, regenerated, and justified. This distinction is crucial for avoiding both legalism, which suggests holiness is a means to earn favor, and antinomianism, which dismisses the pursuit of holiness. The speaker uses the analogy of driving a car versus riding a bike to illustrate the necessity of a precise theological understanding to apply biblical truths effectively in daily life.

The foundation of sanctification is identified as the death and resurrection of Christ. Through baptism into Christ's death, believers are united with Him, enabling them to walk in newness of life. The Holy Spirit creates a new heart and spirit in the believer, resulting in a genuine desire for holiness. The ongoing struggle against sin is presented not as evidence of spiritual death, but as proof of spiritual life, as the new nature conflicts with the old. The lesson concludes by affirming that God, who calls, is faithful to complete the work of sanctification in the believer's spirit, soul, and body.
